item.title: Les USA ont repris le partage de renseignements avec l'Ukraine, dit Zelensky
item.description: Les États-Unis ont repris le partage de renseignements avec l'Ukraine pour l'aider à se défendre contre les attaques de missiles russes, a déclaré dimanche le président Volodimir Zelensky.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les États-Unis ont repris le partage de renseignements avec l'Ukraine pour l'aider à se défendre contre les attaques de missiles russes, a déclaré dimanche le président Volodimir Zelensky. L'Ukraine s'appuie sur les renseignements satellitaires américains pour repérer les missiles tirés quotidiennement par la Russie contre ses villes. Kyiv avait déploré cette semaine que Washington ait cessé de partager ces informations cruciales, après l'accord conclu par Donald Trump avec Moscou sur l'achat de gazole et les pressions exercées par le président américain sur l'Ukraine pour qu'elle cesse ses attaques contre les raffineries russes. S'exprimant dans l'émission "Meet the Press" de la chaîne américaine NBC diffusée dimanche, Volodimir Zelensky a déclaré que le partage de renseignements avait été rétabli. "Nous en sommes très reconnaissants", a-t-il dit.

item.title: UE condena los ataques perpetrados por colonos violentos, incluidos los dirigidos contra diplomáticos: portavoz
item.description: La Unión Europea "condena enérgicamente" los ataques perpetrados por colonos violentos en Cisjordania, incluidos los dirigidos contra diplomáticos europeos, según declaró el domingo el portavoz de política exterior del bloque.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La Unión Europea "condena enérgicamente" los ataques perpetrados por colonos violentos en Cisjordania, incluidos los dirigidos contra diplomáticos europeos, según declaró el domingo el portavoz de política exterior del bloque. La declaración se produjo un día después de que el ministro de Asuntos Exteriores belga, Maxime Prevot, afirmara que colonos israelíes habían atacado a civiles palestinos, a diplomáticos europeos y a un alcalde francés en la Cisjordania ocupada. "Valoramos positivamente las declaraciones de varios representantes israelíes que han condenado los ataques, pero esperamos que se exijan todas las responsabilidades y se adopten medidas efectivas para impedir que continúen los actos de violencia y el acoso violento contra los palestinos —incluso durante la actual temporada de recolección de aceitunas— y contra los periodistas", afirmó el portavoz de la UE.

item.title: Ucrania "lamenta" posible desvío de sus drones sobre Lituania: ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores
item.description: El Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores de Ucrania ha lamentado el posible desvío de sus drones hacia el espacio aéreo lituano el domingo, lo que, según ha señalado, podría haber sido provocado por la guerra electrónica rusa.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: El Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores de Ucrania ha lamentado el posible desvío de sus drones hacia el espacio aéreo lituano el domingo, lo que, según ha señalado, podría haber sido provocado por la guerra electrónica rusa. "Lamentamos el incidente ocurrido esta mañana en el espacio aéreo lituano, que podría haber sido consecuencia de la guerra electrónica rusa, que desvió los drones durante una operación contra objetivos militares legítimos en Rusia", escribió el portavoz Heorhii Tykhyi en X. "Pedimos disculpas por cualquier trastorno, riesgo y preocupación que esto haya podido causar. Nos comprometemos a compartir toda la información relevante con nuestros socios lituanos para esclarecer todas las circunstancias del incidente". En una versión anterior de su publicación también se mencionaba a Letonia.

item.title: Romanian F-16 fighter jets shoot down two drones over Romanian territorial waters
item.description: Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters on Saturday, the defence ministry said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters on Saturday, the defence ministry said. Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Sunday the drones were likely latest generation Russian drones, flying at speeds similar to fighter jets. "The ones from last night were flying at 450 km/h, which leads us to think they were Russian-made Geran-4 drones with a turboprop engine," Miruta said. "This is the first time we've shot down drones like these." The drones were [USN:L8N4610EC TEXT:"brought down"] days after two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania's Black Sea coast, the latest in a series of attacks highlighting risks to commercial shipping on NATO's eastern flank. Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is an export route for Ukraine. NATO member Romania shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, and has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Romania started [USN:L8N43Q0KW TEXT:"shooting down drones"] that enter its space earlier this year. The defence ministry said the two drones entered Romanian waters in the Black Sea on Saturday at 1459 GMT and 1501 GMT, respectively. "NATO is ready and able to react to any potential threat, 24/7, to safeguard our territory and protect our people," a NATO official told Reuters. Romania's Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said the North Atlantic Council will have a meeting on Tuesday to discuss Black Sea defence and deterrence. The two tankers struck earlier this week were hit by Russian drones, a NATO military source told Reuters. Romanian officials are still [USN:L8N4620JP TEXT:"searching"] for seven missing crew members. At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring Bulgaria in the past two weeks, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents occurred outside NATO territorial waters. In Moldova, on Romania's northeast border, officials said a new drone had crashed in a northern district, near the border with Ukraine. Officials said there were no casualties or damage and specialists were trying to determine the drone's origin. Five drones identified as Russian [USN:L1N46210E TEXT:"fell on Moldovan territory"] in a little more than 17 hours on Thursday and Friday, prompting the foreign ministry to issue a statement denouncing Russian actions.

item.title: US resumes intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after pause, Zelenskiy says
item.description: Speaking to NBC's Meet the Press, Zelenskiy said intelligence-sharing was interrupted and later "de-blocked."
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The United States has resumed providing Ukraine critical intelligence to help it defend against Russian missile strikes, after a brief pause, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in comments published on Sunday. Ukraine has relied on US intelligence to spot the fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia has fired in waves at its cities. US President Donald Trump had [USN:L1N45Z16F TEXT:"said earlier this week"] that Washington was still sharing intelligence, although Ukrainian officials said some Russian strikes had occurred without warning. Speaking to NBC's Meet the Press, Zelenskiy said intelligence-sharing had been interrupted but later "de-blocked." "We are very thankful for this," he said. "Now it works." But Zelenskiy said other US actions, such as signing a deal to import Russian diesel and [USN:L6N464042 TEXT:"waiving sanctions on Russia"] that had been slated to take effect this week, will hurt Ukraine. "If the United States will officially take the side of Russia, of course if these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail and we will not be able to stand," he said. Over the past week, a [USN:L6N46303A TEXT:"widening rift"] between Trump and Zelenskiy has sparked concerns that their tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Zelenskiy told NBC that he hopes Trump will remain an ally of Ukraine. "We want to trust him, and I hope that he will change his decisions," Zelenskiy said. "Because I think that it's all mistakes and it will not help us. And it will not help United States." In a Truth Social post on Sunday afternoon, Trump wrote that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything "that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." Ukraine gets US help that Russia does not receive, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told NBC, citing intelligence-sharing and the provision of US munitions to other countries for resale to Ukraine. But Bessent, speaking with "Meet the Press" after it aired Zelenskiy's interview, did not directly answer when asked multiple times whether the United States views Ukraine as an ally. "Zelenskiy presents a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win," Bessent said. "The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement."

item.title: Hurricane Trudy lashes Mexico's Pacific coast, but is set to weaken tonight
item.description: Hurricane Trudy brought heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Mexico's southwest and west-central regions early on Sunday as it maintained its strength and tracked parallel to the country's Pacific coast.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Hurricane Trudy brought heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Mexico's southwest and west-central regions early on Sunday as it maintained its strength and tracked parallel to the country's Pacific coast. The US National Hurricane Center said Trudy was about 150 miles (240 km) west of Manzanillo, with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 kph). Trudy was moving northwest at about 10 mph (17 kph) and is forecast to remain near the coast through Sunday evening before weakening overnight and moving south of Baja California Sur on Monday and Tuesday. "Little change in strength is expected this morning, but rapid weakening is forecast to begin by tonight," the NHC said. Trudy is expected to bring four to eight inches (10 to 20 cm) of rain, with isolated totals of around 12 inches, across parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in steep terrain. The NHC reiterated warnings of dangerous storm surge accompanied by damaging waves in areas exposed to onshore winds along parts of Mexico's Pacific coast.

item.title: Oil lifts Saudi bourse; Egypt tumbles on regional tensions
item.description: Gulf markets ended mixed on Sunday as geopolitical tensions weighed. Saudi Arabia was lifted by higher oil prices, while Qatar fell to a six-year low and Egypt slipped as it was drawn further into the Middle East turmoil.
item.dc:creator: Ateeq Shariff
item.content:encoded: Gulf markets ended mixed on Sunday as geopolitical tensions weighed. Saudi Arabia was lifted by higher oil prices, while Qatar fell to a six-year low and Egypt slipped as it was drawn further into the Middle East turmoil. Saudi Arabia's benchmark index (.TASI) rose 0.8%, led by a 2.1% rise in oil behemoth Saudi Aramco (2222.SE) . Oil prices supported the move. On Friday, Brent crude futures settled up $3.94, or 3.7%, higher at $109.86, their highest since May 19. Traders feared that rising tensions in the Middle East could further tighten supply. They were also assessing how much diesel Russia could supply to the global market. In Qatar, the index (.QSI) fell 2% to 8,634, its lowest close since April 2020. Petrochemical maker Industries Qatar (IQCD.QA) declined 4.3%, and sharia-compliant lender Qatar Islamic Bank (QISB.QA) shed 2.6%. On the diplomatic front, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media on Sunday that Tehran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days was [USN:L1N46401N TEXT:"still on the table"]. Outside the Gulf, Egypt's blue-chip index (.EGX30) declined 2.6%, its biggest intraday fall since February. The Egyptian presidency [USN:L1N46401H TEXT:"said"] Cairo is ready to give Saudi Arabia the support it needs to defend its security and stability. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have intensified their attacks on the world's largest oil exporter. Saudi Arabia (.TASI) advanced 0.8% to 10,190 Qatar (.QSI) retreated 2% to 8,634 Egypt (.EGX30) declined 2.6% to 50,896 Bahrain (.BAX) dropped 0.5% to 1,899 Oman (.MSX30) eased 0.3% to 7,656 Kuwait (.BKP) fell 0.2% to 8,871

item.title: Chwalinska outwits Kartal to win Wuhan Open
item.description: French Open finalist Maja Chwalinska won her first title on the WTA tour as she shook off early nerves to beat Sonay Kartal 2-6 6-4 6-2 at the Wuhan Open final on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: French Open finalist Maja Chwalinska won her first title on the WTA tour as she shook off early nerves to beat Sonay Kartal 2-6 6-4 6-2 at the Wuhan Open final on Sunday. Left-hander Chwalinska deployed a defensive right-handed lob to disrupt Kartal's flow and outwitted the Briton with clever changes of direction and winners into the corners. Briton Kartal, 170th in the WTA rankings and the lowest-ranked finalist in a WTA 1000 tournament, dominated the first set with powerful forehands as her Polish opponent's drop shots and slices kept landing wide. But Chwalinska, fresh off a win over [USN:L6N46303P TEXT:"childhood friend Iga Swiatek"], fought back in the second set, dragging Kartal into long rallies and earning three breaks to force a decider. Under pressure, Kartal struggled with netted returns in the third set, making 11 unforced errors as an emboldened Chwalinska won four games in a row to clinch victory. "That was one heck of a battle," said Kartal, who returned from a six-month injury layoff last month and is expected to break into the top-50 in the rankings. Chwalinska, who became [USN:L4N42C1MW TEXT:"the first qualifier "] to reach the French Open final in June, credited her coaches for their help during the best year in the 25-year-old's career, where she started as 146th in the world and is now likely to rise to a career-high 11th. "I am very grateful for every person in my life, basically," she said.

item.title: Ukraine 'regrets' possible diversion of its drones over Lithuania, foreign ministry says
item.description: Ukraine's foreign ministry said it regretted the possible diversion of its drones into Lithuanian airspace on Sunday, which it said may have been caused by Russian electronic warfare.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ukraine's foreign ministry said it regretted the possible diversion of its drones into Lithuanian airspace on Sunday, which it said may have been caused by Russian electronic warfare. "We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia," spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi wrote on X. "We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused. We are committed to sharing all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident." A prior version of his post also mentioned Latvia.

item.title: Macron llama a la calma mientras Francia evalúa consecuencias de peores disturbios en últimos años
item.description: El presidente Emmanuel Macron hizo un llamado a la calma el domingo, un día después de que Francia viviera uno de sus peores días de disturbios en años, con miles de detenidos y tiendas saqueadas o dañadas tras las protestas por los altos precios y el deterioro de los servicios públicos.
item.dc:creator: Sybille de La Hamaide
item.content:encoded: El presidente Emmanuel Macron hizo un llamado a la calma el domingo, un día después de que Francia viviera uno de sus peores días de disturbios en años, con miles de detenidos y tiendas saqueadas o dañadas tras las protestas por los altos precios y el deterioro de los servicios públicos. Se produjeron nuevos enfrentamientos en París y Marsella, donde la policía antidisturbios intervino para impedir los intentos de saqueo de comercios. Las manifestaciones a nivel nacional se habían convertido en disturbios el sábado, con un ayuntamiento incendiado, tiendas saqueadas y edificios cubiertos de grafitis, mientras grupos violentos se enfrentaban a la policía en ciudades de todo el país. "Al ver estas imágenes, todos nos hemos preguntado: ¿qué les pasaba por la cabeza? ¿Cómo pueden los franceses hacerle esto a Francia?", declaró Macron en un discurso televisado dirigido a la nación. "Nada lo justifica, nada lo explica, nada lo excusa. Esta noche, todos sentimos ira y vergüenza". Los disturbios del sábado pusieron de manifiesto la profunda ira hacia Macron, que dejará el cargo en 2027 tras una década en el poder que se ha caracterizado cada vez más por el descontento social, una economía débil y una deuda galopante. Macron afirmó que quienes protestaban pacíficamente tenían motivos legítimos de queja y que sus acciones no debían confundirse con las de quienes buscaban sembrar el caos. No llegó a declarar el estado de emergencia, tal y como exigían algunos políticos de derecha, pero afirmó que el Gobierno tomaría medidas para permitir a los prefectos prohibir las manifestaciones si fuera necesario para proteger los edificios públicos y los comercios locales. LAS MANIFESTACIONES EN PARÍS, "COMO UNA ZONA DE GUERRA" El Gobierno ha achacado la violencia a lo que, según afirma, son grupos de extrema izquierda, así como a delincuentes que, según afirma, habrían instigado los saqueos. Un manifestante falleció el sábado tras sufrir un paro cardíaco durante las manifestaciones en París. La policía llevó a cabo 2.400 detenciones en toda Francia, mientras que casi 1.000 agentes resultaron heridos, según informó el ministro del Interior francés, Laurent Núñez. La policía volvió a enfrentarse a los manifestantes y lanzó gases lacrimógenos en la Place de la République el domingo por la tarde, mientras los manifestantes prendían fuego a montones de bicicletas. Un testigo de Reuters afirmó que parecía haber varios cientos de manifestantes en la zona. Se llevó a cabo una operación de limpieza a gran escala en ciudades desde Lille, en el norte, hasta Marsella, en el sur, y desde Estrasburgo, en el este, hasta Burdeos, en el suroeste, donde una turba enmascarada irrumpió en la residencia del prefecto local. «¡Esto parece una zona de guerra!», exclamó el empresario neerlandés Tije De Boer, que visitaba París con sus hijos y afirmó que los disturbios le obligaron a evacuar su hotel en la Place de la République. Más de medio millón de personas se sumaron el sábado a las marchas en decenas de ciudades, lo que supuso la convergencia de un movimiento estudiantil que lleva un mes en marcha con un descontento social más amplio contra el aumento del coste de la vida y el deterioro de los servicios públicos. VARIOS CIENTOS DE TIENDAS DAÑADAS Mientras cientos de miles de personas se manifestaban pacíficamente por toda Francia el sábado, grupos marginales violentos atacaron edificios públicos, saquearon boutiques de lujo y supermercados, y atacaron vehículos y agentes de policía. La líder de extrema derecha del Agrupación Nacional, Marine Le Pen, favorita de cara a la campaña presidencial del año que viene, también hizo un llamamiento a la calma, afirmando que Francia no debe acostumbrarse a las imágenes de un país maltratado, abusado y saqueado. "La violencia no es una opinión. La destrucción no es una forma de expresión. Y el caos no puede servir de proyecto para Francia", afirmó en un discurso grabado en vídeo. El candidato presidencial de extrema izquierda de "Francia Indómita", Jean-Luc Mélenchon, señaló que Macron debía dar respuesta a las reivindicaciones de los estudiantes de secundaria que se manifestaban. En Limoges, famosa por su porcelana, el derrumbe de la torre del reloj del ayuntamiento en medio de un intenso incendio reavivó los recuerdos del incendio de 2019 que devastó la catedral de Notre Dame de París. El alcalde, Guillaume Guerin, señaló que no se habían desplegado suficientes agentes de la policía nacional en su ciudad. "Hubo una clara intención premeditada de incendiar el ayuntamiento, y las personas que se encontraban en su interior temían por sus vidas", declaró Guerin a Reuters el domingo. Amenazó con dimitir si la ciudad no recibía los fondos necesarios para reparar el ayuntamiento. El ministro de Economía, Roland Lescure, se comprometió el domingo a apoyar a los propietarios de negocios que sufrieron pérdidas. "Quienes causen daños pagarán, repararán los daños y rendirán cuentas por su intención de sembrar el caos", afirmó Lescure en un comunicado. El director general de la cadena minorista francesa Carrefour (CARR.PA) , Alexandre Bompard, declaró a la cadena francesa BFMTV que 50 de las tiendas de la empresa habían sufrido daños, incluidas 20 que fueron saqueadas, y que las pérdidas por los daños ascendían a decenas de millones de euros.

item.title: Papa León se compromete a reincorporarse gradualmente a sus funciones en primer acto tras operación de cáncer
item.description: El papa León se comprometió el domingo a reanudar poco a poco sus actividades habituales como líder de los 1.400 millones de católicos del mundo, mientras saludaba a la multitud en la Plaza de San Pedro durante su primer acto público desde que se sometiera a una intervención quirúrgica por cáncer de pulmón hace cinco días.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee
item.content:encoded: El papa León se comprometió el domingo a reanudar poco a poco sus actividades habituales como líder de los 1.400 millones de católicos del mundo, mientras saludaba a la multitud en la Plaza de San Pedro durante su primer acto público desde que se sometiera a una intervención quirúrgica por cáncer de pulmón hace cinco días. El pontífice, de 71 años, fue operado el martes para extirparle el lóbulo inferior del pulmón derecho, lo que ha avivado las especulaciones sobre cómo su enfermedad podría afectar a sus 17 meses de papado. Sonriendo desde una ventana del Palacio Apostólico del Vaticano mientras se dirigía a los peregrinos que se encontraban abajo con voz firme y clara el domingo, el primer papa estadounidense agradeció a personas de todo el mundo sus oraciones y afirmó que ahora comenzaría a retomar su agenda habitual. "Tras haber superado esta delicada fase… ahora retomaré gradualmente mis actividades, siempre con la ayuda de Dios y vuestras oraciones", afirmó Leon. El papa, que recibió el alta del hospital Gemelli de Roma el sábado, se asomó a la ventana del palacio sin ayuda y celebró su cita semanal del mediodía como de costumbre. También instó a los peregrinos que esperaban abajo bajo un cielo nublado a dejar de lado cualquier ambición egoísta y a servir a Dios "sin concesiones". UNA MONJA LLORA AL VER APARECER A LEON A León le han diagnosticado un adenocarcinoma de pulmón, el tipo más común de cáncer de pulmón. El diagnóstico, para el papa más joven en décadas —elegido apenas en mayo de 2025—, causó conmoción. Sus médicos le dieron el alta el sábado después de que los análisis de sangre y las pruebas de imagen torácicas realizados ese mismo día mostraran que se encontraba lo suficientemente bien como para volver a casa. Afirmaron que era capaz de realizar sus actividades diarias normales de forma autónoma. La multitud reunida en la Plaza de San Pedro, que según el Vaticano ascendía a unas 15.000 personas, gritó y aplaudió con fuerza cuando León se asomó por primera vez a la ventana el domingo. Una monja católica se arrodilló y lloró, cubriéndose el rostro con la mano. A pocos pasos de allí, un grupo de otras monjas sostenía en alto un cartel en el que se leía: "Mis mejores deseos, Santo Padre. Te queremos y rezamos por ti". LA AGENDA DEL PAPA EN CONSTANTE CAMBIO León suele tener una agenda muy apretada, pero el Vaticano ha cancelado sus demás actos públicos al menos hasta el miércoles, día en que tiene previsto celebrar la audiencia general semanal en la Plaza de San Pedro. No se ha confirmado si celebrará dicha audiencia. El Papa también tiene previsto visitar Uruguay, Argentina y Perú del 6 al 17 de noviembre, en uno de los viajes más intensos organizados para un líder católico en décadas. El doctor Stefano Margaritora, cirujano jefe del Papa, afirmó el sábado que León podría haberse recuperado por completo a tiempo para ese viaje. Sin embargo, el cardenal Pietro Parolin, secretario de Estado del Vaticano, se ha mostrado escéptico. El viernes declaró a los periodistas que es posible que el papa tenga que ajustar el ritmo de su agenda de aquí en adelante "en función de su estado de salud".

item.title: Carney’s pipeline push is unlikely to bring back Canada’s oil jobs boom
item.description: Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney is betting a new pipeline can help revive the country’s oil industry, boost its production and exports, and reduce its dependence on the United States.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Stephenson
item.content:encoded: Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney is betting a new pipeline can help revive the country’s oil industry, boost its production and exports, and reduce its dependence on the United States. Bringing back jobs will be much harder. In the Alberta oil hub of Fort McMurray – nicknamed Fort McMoney in its heyday more than a decade ago – the tens of thousands of oil field jobs that powered the last boom are unlikely to return, even if Carney gets his pipeline. Instead, much of the growth in oil sands output is likely to come from automation and efficiency gains rather than large-scale hiring, according to industry forecasts and nearly a dozen interviews with company officials, workers, politicians and academics. The [USN:S0N41N000 TEXT:"pipeline "]backed by Carney would transport 1 million barrels of crude oil a day to a port on the Pacific coast, expanding export capacity to Asia. Asked by Reuters what the pipeline would mean for the region’s economy, Carney – a former central banker – cautioned against anticipating a return to the oil-boom days. "I wouldn't use the term 'boom'," Carney said during a visit to Fort McMurray this month. "I would use ‘sustained growth’." MORE OIL, FEWER WORKERS More oil without many more permanent jobs could leave Carney politically exposed on two fronts: Critics on the left say his efforts to fast-track the project’s regulatory approval risks sacrificing the environment, while those on the right argue the deregulation should deliver faster economic growth, higher salaries and more oil jobs. Low job growth could also further fuel Alberta’s separatist movement, though a referendum on whether to hold a vote to leave Canada is expected to fail on Monday. An August labor forecast by industry group Energy Safety Canada projects that oil sands employment will fall by 920 jobs or 4% by 2035, even as production grows 6%. A spokesperson for Energy Safety Canada told Reuters that a new West Coast pipeline would likely reverse the projected job decline but may not add many permanent jobs because of the “structural trend” of producing more oil with fewer workers. "Nobody should expect that something that happened 15 years ago will happen the same way today," said Dianna De Sousa, CEO of the Fort McMurray Chamber of Commerce. A spokesperson for Carney declined to comment on the lackluster projections for job creation from the pipeline, referring questions to the Department of Natural Resources, which did not respond. FROM BOOM TO BUST TO WILDFIRES From 2000 to 2014, Canadian and international oil companies spent billions to build out the mega-mines and other facilities required to extract bitumen, the thick oil found in northern Alberta. Fort McMurray became a place where workers fresh out of high school could earn six-figure salaries, putting new pickups and pricey boats in their driveways. Fly-in, fly-out workers — some from as far as 5,000 km (3,107 miles) away – packed on-site work camps because the city lacked housing. Then came the 2015 oil price crash, followed by a devastating wildfire one year later. Investors’ growing focus on environmental, social and governance (ESG) criteria combined with the climate policies of Carney's predecessor Justin Trudeau deepened the slump. International oil majors exited. Annual oil sands capital investment fell from a C$35 billion ($24.55 billion) peak in 2014 to C$14.2 billion in 2024, according to Statistics Canada. The last major new oil sands project, Suncor's Fort Hills, started up in 2018. Alberta’s oil and gas sector employs 435,000 people today, including temporary and part-time workers, 85,000 fewer than in 2014, according to data from Alberta’s Servus Credit Union. Real disposable income in the province is still 10% below 2014 levels. Housing values have declined sharply. Stronger oil prices and rising production have brought some signs of recovery, including regional population growth for the first time in a decade. But flights from Calgary and other major cities sometimes arrive nearly empty, and vacant commercial spaces dot downtown. "Things are not getting better," said Jenny Parsons, who has worked as a truck driver and contractor at oil sands sites since moving from Newfoundland 15 years ago. She said she was earning barely a dollar more an hour than she was in 2011. WHAT A PIPELINE COULD BRING No oil sands company has committed the C$100 billion in private investment needed to fill the proposed pipeline and build the [USN:S0N43F051 TEXT:"carbon capture"] and storage project Carney has made a condition of federal approval. Kendall Dilling, head of the Oil Sands Alliance, which represents the five largest companies, said the projects could create thousands of jobs across Canada by the mid-2030s, including upstream investment and supply-chain activity as well as pipeline construction. But many of these jobs would be temporary construction jobs, in British Columbia as well as Alberta, rather than permanent oil-industry jobs. Some of those jobs no longer exist. Efficiency gains, for example, have cut the time oil companies spend on routine maintenance, which has reduced the number of staff as well as contract positions, he said. The employment gains “may be less than the absolute peaks that we've seen in the past.” Jason Kenney, Alberta's conservative premier from 2019 to 2022, cut corporate taxes to get oil sands companies to spend on big projects. But even after oil prices rose and revenue stabilized, companies prioritized shareholder returns over job growth, he told Reuters. "I was certainly frustrated with them,” he told Reuters. He said he urged companies to allocate some of the tax cut savings to their capital plans. "The people need to see a benefit, not just the shareholder in New York." The industry group representing oil companies did not respond directly to Kenney's comments but said the pipeline provided an opportunity to increase production, create jobs and grow government revenue. CARNEY FACES RISKS FROM LEFT AND RIGHT By backing a new pipeline, Carney — who grew up in Alberta's capital of Edmonton — has brokered an uneasy truce between the federal government and Alberta conservatives. But he has angered some in his own Liberal party by embracing oil to help the Canadian economy survive President Donald Trump’s tariffs. He has repealed many of Trudeau's environmental policies, [USN:L1N4570FS TEXT:"cut the tax rate "]on new capital investment, and is promoting Canadian oil to investors abroad. While Carney’s approval rating was at 62% in a September poll from Angus Reid, public sentiment on energy and the environment can shift quickly. "It's important to remember that the environmental policies of Justin Trudeau were widely popular at the time," said Lori Williams, a political science professor at Calgary’s Mount Royal University. "If we see more environmentally friendly options starting to come on in the future then I think additional pipelines in Canada will be much harder to sell." Fort McMurray's boom had its downsides. The flood of workers strained local infrastructure and created tensions between locals and the thousands of people in work camps. Some oil sands companies now hire more locals to reduce their reliance on fly-in workers, a shift that reflects a leaner but steadier industry. Still, longtime residents like Colin Hartigan, owner of the city’s Coldwell Banker United office, hope that Carney's ambitions will bring back at least an echo of the old Fort McMurray. "At some point, there's going to be another boom," Hartigan said. "Do I think families here want to see that? Not like in the past, that was a little bit crazy. But do we all pray for it? Absolutely."

item.title: Samsung to use TSMC technology for Nvidia's next-generation memory chips, Seoul newspaper reports
item.description: Samsung Electronics will use TSMC's 3-nanometre process to produce base dies for Nvidia's next-generation custom high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, the Seoul Economic Daily reported on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) will use TSMC's (2330.TW) 3-nanometre process to produce base dies for Nvidia's (NVDA.O) next-generation custom high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, the Seoul Economic Daily reported on Sunday. The move would mark the first time Samsung has worked with the Taiwanese contract chipmaker at the HBM manufacturing stage, according to the report. Nvidia has asked Samsung, SK Hynix (000660.KS) and Micron Technology (MU.O) to use TSMC's process for NVHBM base dies, and sixth-generation DRAM technology for its core dies, the newspaper said, citing industry sources. NVHBM, unveiled in August, integrates Nvidia's custom memory controller into the base die and is aimed at standardising implementation across multiple memory suppliers, according to the company. Samsung accepted Nvidia's requirements after an internal review but plans to retain its in-house production model for standard HBM and custom products for other customers, Seoul Economic Daily said. It is also assessing whether its own foundry could produce NVHBM base dies if demand exceeds TSMC's capacity, the newspaper quoted an unnamed source as saying.

item.title: Turkey will get some diesel from US-Russia supply deal, energy minister says
item.description: Turkey will take some of the diesel Russia is supplying to global markets under its agreement with US President Donald Trump, Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Turkey will take some of the diesel Russia is supplying to global markets under its agreement with US President Donald Trump, Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said on Sunday. Bayraktar said the US-Russia [USN:L8N4610WB TEXT:"diesel supply deal"] was important in terms of energy security for Turkey. Ankara relies on Russia for some of its energy needs, as well as on Iran, Azerbaijan and others. It is trying to diversify through deals with the US and other partners. "Russia imposed restrictions on diesel exports in recent months when they started experiencing this problem. Now they reached a diesel deal with Trump... Through the talks we held, we will take some of that diesel to Turkey," Bayraktar told broadcaster Kanal 7. He did not elaborate. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European officials and some of Trump's fellow [USN:L1N45Z0VJ TEXT:"Republican politicians"] strongly criticised the deal. Bayraktar also said that Turkey plans to bring a second floating gas production platform online in the first quarter of 2028, adding that the platform would bring Turkey's daily output in the Black Sea to 45 million cubic metres. On Saturday, Turkey sent its [USN:L8N4611PM TEXT:"first floating gas production platform"], the Osman Gazi, to the Black Sea, a move Bayraktar has said is expected to roughly double daily output from its largest domestic gas field, the Sakarya field, to 20 million cubic metres from the current 9.5 million, equivalent to 7.3 billion cubic metres (bcm) annually. "In the first quarter of 2028, the second floating production platform is coming to Turkey and we will carry out 25 million cubic metres of production with it. It has a slightly bigger capacity (than Osman Gazi)," he said. "Therefore, with 45 million cubic metres, we will be using our own gas in three out of four homes in Turkey." He added that Turkey's daily production at the field would increase to 550,000 barrels of oil equivalent with the second floating platform. Turkey is one of Europe's largest gas markets, consuming 59 bcm last year. The country relies on imports for almost all its gas needs, with domestic production totalling 3.1 bcm last year, most of it from the Sakarya field. Bayraktar also said [USN:A4N3DZ01O TEXT:"hydrocarbon exploration operations"] planned off Pakistan had been delayed by about six months due to the Iran war's impact on the region.

item.title: In France's Limoges, the fire-ravaged town hall rekindles memories of Notre Dame
item.description: The 19th-century neo-Renaissance building survived two world wars.
item.dc:creator: Clotaire Achi
item.content:encoded: Residents in Limoges recoiled in horror on Sunday at the city's fire-ravaged town hall, an ornate 19th century neo-Renaissance building which survived two world wars but was torched by a masked mob during the [USN:L1N46302B TEXT:"worst unrest"] to convulse France in years. Stunned onlookers had watched helplessly the previous evening as the blaze tore through the roof, felling the building's clock tower in scenes that revived haunting memories of the collapse of Notre Dame cathedral's spire in a 2019 fire. "It broke my heart. I saw Notre Dame all over again, except this time it was our town," said Francoise Faurie who witnessed the fire consume Limoges' town hall. Faurie's family had been due to celebrate her grand-daughter's baptism in the town hall in a month's time. "What kind of country are we living in? What are we leaving our children?" she said. "There's no reason to touch that building. You can have demands, you have the right to protest, but not the right to violence." EXTENSIVE DAMAGE The local prefect, Maurice Barate, said the roof had caved in onto lower floors, sparing only the west wing, and that large parts of the exterior had been destroyed. The destruction of the building, a listed monument that opened in 1883 and was inspired by Paris' city hall, was a "heritage catastrophe", he said. Its central clock tower and belfry towered 43 metres (141 feet) over the square below. "It's inadmissible to have burned down the town hall!" one local resident, Gilbert, said. "Those who did this need to be punished. They need to pay out of their own pocket, it's not for the state to pay." The town's shaken mayor, Guillaume Guerin, described how the local police force had quickly been overwhelmed by several hundred-strong mob who he said smashed windows and used a battering ram to break down the main door. "The logistics, the organisation, the premeditation behind yesterday’s attack on the town hall is something I find unbearable," he told reporters. Guerin said there had been insufficient police numbers to protect the building since officers from the national force had been deployed to the street protest. "I had no single national police officer to protect the town hall," the centre-right mayor continued. "This country is doing badly, this country is doing very badly, and it’s a small provincial mayor telling you so." Crowds gathered under blue skies as specialists surveyed the damage. Edith Lorcen, a retired nurse, expressed her shock at the malice of those behind the attack. "I'm disgusted. I'm hurting," Lorcen said. "But it does nothing to add hate on top of hate."

item.title: Davidovich Fokina overcomes Jodar to claim Shanghai crown
item.description: Alejandro Davidovich Fokina ended Rafael Jodar's dream run at the Shanghai Masters on Sunday, battling back to beat his fellow Spaniard 1-6 7-6(5) 6-4 and clinch the biggest title of his career.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Alejandro Davidovich Fokina ended Rafael Jodar's dream run at the Shanghai Masters on Sunday, battling back to beat his fellow Spaniard 1-6 7-6(5) 6-4 and clinch the biggest title of his career. The 25th-seeded Davidovich Fokina is set to climb 13 places to a career-high world number 13 when the rankings are released on Monday. Jodar, playing in his first Masters 1000 final and the youngest Shanghai finalist in tournament history, made a blistering start, broke for a 2-0 lead and again to take the opening set. Davidovich Fokina recovered from a break down in the second set and saved break points in three successive service games before edging a tight tiebreak to force a decider. The momentum swung decisively in Davidovich Fokina's favour when he broke the 12th-seeded Jodar twice and sealed victory in two hours and 27 minutes. "I have a blank mind," Davidovich Fokina said. "I don't know what to say and I don't know how I feel. Just a huge relief. "After the first set I had to keep trying, keep pushing. In the tiebreak, I believed in myself again. In the third set, maybe I had a bit more fitness physically." It the third ATP singles title of the 27-year-old's career, adding to his ATP 250 triumphs in Chengdu and Mallorca this season. The first meeting between the two Spaniards pitted one of the ATP Tour's rising talents against a player enjoying the best season of his career. The 20-year-old Jodar, who was ranked outside the world's top 900 little more than a year ago, strengthened his bid to qualify for the ATP Finals in Turin in his first full season on tour.

item.title: India widens cancer drug price caps, lowering prices of 137 medicines
item.description: India will reduce the prices of as many as 137 cancer drugs by 70%, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers said on Saturday, as it widened price controls in a bid to make treatment more affordable.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: India will reduce the prices of as many as 137 cancer drugs by 70%, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers said on Saturday, as it widened price controls in a bid to make treatment more affordable. Trade margins on the drugs will be limited to 30% of the maximum retail price, the ministry added. The medicines, which include immunotherapy drugs used for treating over 20 types of cancer, as well as for breast, prostate, colon, ovarian and cervical cancer, will be subject to the price changes from November 9. The latest decision builds on price controls introduced in 2019 on 42 anti-cancer drugs that cut prices by as much as 90%.

item.title: Albanian PM says protests pose threat to EU membership, not government
item.description: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Sunday rejected calls to step down and said street protests, which continued for a sixth day, were a threat not to his government but to Albania's hopes of joining the European Union.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci
item.content:encoded: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Sunday rejected calls to step down and said street protests, which continued for a sixth day, were a threat not to his government but to Albania's hopes of joining the European Union. Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana and spread to other cities in the past week. Demonstrators demanding Rama's resignation have set fire to government buildings as well as banks, smashed shop windows and pulled up paving stones to throw at police. Violence erupted again on Sunday when thousands gathered outside the Education Ministry and hurled rocks at riot police who responded with tear gas, water cannon and [USN:L6N46303U TEXT:"rubber bullets"]. The unrest, which followed months of largely peaceful protests over the summer [USN:L6N42J18T TEXT:"against a luxury coastal development"] backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, poses the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and last year won a fourth term in office. "I am not being challenged, the government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged," Rama said in a live address on Facebook. “Albanians need to think very clearly: Do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?” EU CONDEMNS USE OF VIOLENCE IN PROTESTS Rama invited students to talks as excavators dug up and removed the paving outside his office in central Tirana before protests started on Sunday. "This will not absolutely stop the protesters. This is just made to remove any way of protection of the protesters from the police. This is just that," said Elton Prendi, 40, a Tirana resident. The European Commission [USN:FWN4630JL TEXT:"condemned "]the use of violence in Tirana and other cities and welcomed authorities' commitment to protect people's right to protest. Rama canceled a meeting with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker in Vienna scheduled for Monday, the Austrian chancellery said. Corruption scandals have tarnished Albania's image over the years and analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking. However, Rama has said his government is tackling corruption as never before. Along with Montenegro, Albania is currently leading the posse of Balkan countries seeking to join the EU, and is aiming for entry by 2030. Rama blamed unspecified foreign interests for the protests and for what he said was an attempted drone attack at his office this week. "God knows what the consequences will be. There are no young people, no students, and no minors who would even think of implementing this plan. This is a foreign hand," he said. Police said 388 people had been charged with criminal offences during the demonstrations. Scores of police officers and protesters have been injured.

item.title: One killed, 15 injured in Ukrainian drone attack on St Petersburg and Leningrad region
item.description: Ukrainian drones struck oil facilities and logistics and data centers, local authorities said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: One person was killed and 15 were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on oil facilities, logistics and data centres in Russia's St Petersburg and the Leningrad region, local authorities said on Sunday. St Petersburg's governor Alexander Beglov said fires had broken out at the St Petersburg oil terminal, an oil depot and industrial warehouses. Russian e-commerce company Ozon said that its logistics hub in St Petersburg was on fire and the internet company VK (VKCO.MM) said that its data centre in the Leningrad region had been attacked by drones, but services were available to users as normal. Ukrainian drone producer Fire Point said on Sunday that the Ukrainian military had struck a VK data centre near St Petersburg. Russian air defence units downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, the Russian Defence Ministry said. Russia is constantly responding to Ukrainian attacks with systematic, large-scale strikes, the TASS news agency reported on Sunday, citing Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. "The Kyiv regime is resisting. But this cannot change the course of events," he said, answering a question about how Russia might respond to Kyiv's attack on St Petersburg.

item.title: IMF/World Bank meetings leave developing countries with more questions than answers
item.description: Last week's meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading Middle East war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Shalal, David Lawder
item.content:encoded: Last week's meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading Middle East war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble. Not for the first time, [USN:L1N46302K TEXT:"lower-income countries"] are being rocked by the spillover from the actions of wealthier nations: rising debt service costs, higher inflation and the risk of falling ever further behind economically thanks to the AI boom. What they got was the stock advice the global lenders always dish out: to shrink fiscal deficits and accelerate economic reforms to attract more private sector investment. Kristalina Georgieva, the first IMF chief from a developing nation - Bulgaria - said advanced economies were in fact the worst offenders on budget imbalances. She noted that developing countries' debt levels had actually fallen in recent years, only for surging bond yields elsewhere to drive up their borrowing costs. Average debt service payments there had more than doubled from a decade ago to 14% of government revenue, crowding out education, healthcare and other critical areas, she said. ADVANCED ECONOMIES FOCUSED ON THEIR OWN PROBLEMS At a panel on Saturday, Georgieva said many issues remained unresolved, especially around AI: "We are in a place where we have many more questions than we have answers. And my alert to everybody is: Do not fall for the guys that pretend they have the answers. They are tricking you." Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council think tank, said the meetings had flunked their opportunity to come up with guidance or ways to help. "It's hard to talk about the developing world when the advanced economies don't have their act together and are at risk of a fiscal crisis," he said. "And that's on top of political situations in many of these countries that makes development aid not a priority at the moment." Mauricio Cardenas, Colombia's former finance minister and now a research scholar at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs in New York, said many policymakers were left with a deep sense that "something really bad could happen" but no real roadmap to navigate the future. "The IMF and World Bank are not particularly well prepared for this new phase. They understand that something is going on, they bring in experts on AI," he said. "But in the end, there's no kind of specific, concrete advice on how to be prepared for something where you don't really understand how it's going to unfold." The geopolitical tensions that have roiled both institutions since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - complicating concerted action - were also evident in Bangkok when nearly half the delegates at an [USN:L1N46301V TEXT:"IMF steering committee"] walked out when Russia's finance minister spoke. Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport delayed the arrival of the head of that committee, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who had to travel overland to Qatar to catch a flight. And Bangkok itself was a stark reminder of the challenges facing developing countries, still partly under water after floods in September that caused almost $200 million in damage to Thailand's industrial sector. RISING INEQUALITY COULD RAISE COSTS IN LONG TERM Kate Pickett, a professor at the University of York, urged policymakers to focus on more inclusive growth rather than forcing developing countries into tough structural reforms. "If inequality increases, if poverty deepens, that will increase their costs in the long term," she said. "It's not enough to describe an economy as resilient. It's only resilient for the rich and the privileged.” Ayhan Kose, deputy chief economist at the World Bank, said the global economy had weathered its biggest energy shock - from the US-Israeli war on Iran - better than expected. But while a global recession had been avoided, he said growth outlooks in both developing and advanced economies were worse than before. Growth had already fallen off in half of advanced economies, while in developing countries as a whole, it had slowed significantly to around 3.6% from 4.4%. “People are really worried because resilience today is not a guarantee for resilience tomorrow," he said. "Now they are worried about what will be the next shock, because every six months, if not every three months, there is a new shock." While no specific initiatives were announced, he said the World Bank remained focused on helping developing countries prepare for advancements in AI, in part by mobilising more private capital, now at triple the levels of 2022. Yet it, too, has to contend with sharp drops in official development aid and persistent challenges in attracting foreign investment to developing countries. “The reality on the ground is the reality on the ground,” he said.
